narrative_brief:
🧩 拼圖遊戲：建構你的 SDG Pecha Kucha 演講！
透過這個互動式拼圖，你將掌握成功進行 SDG Pecha Kucha 簡報的核心邏輯。

第一步：掌握演講架構 (Master the Framework)
首先，請熟悉 SDG Pecha Kucha 的六大核心脈絡：Part 1 引言 (Introduction)、Part 2 問題指認 (Problem Identification)、Part 3 成果與進展 (Achievements & Progress)、Part 4 解決方案 (Solutions)、Part 5 影響與未來挑戰 (Implications & Future Challenges)、Part 6 結語與行動呼籲 (Conclusion & Call to Action)。

第二步：20 秒限時挑戰 (The 20-Second Challenge)
你會收到 20 段獨立的「20 秒講稿」。你的任務是：
👉 精準判斷： 根據內容關鍵字，辨識該片段屬於哪一個部分。
👉 邏輯拼湊： 將片段歸位，完整還原整場 6 分 40 秒的演說。

第三步：回饋與深思 (Review & Reflect)
完成拼圖後，對照正確答案並思考：
✔ 為什麼這段話具備該階段的特徵？
✔ 優秀的簡報如何透過轉折與銜接建構嚴謹的說服力？

stages.source_description: Introduction (Slides 1-3: Hook, SDG 4 definition, Taiwan context with critical setup)

title.zh: 挑戰教育公平性

A2.text: Good morning. Is school in Taiwan fair for every child? Today we look at SDG 4, Quality Education. On paper we look great, but science class tells a different story.
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: Good morning. To start, let’s look at a big question: is education in Taiwan truly fair for everyone? Today, we will discuss SDG 4, which is about Quality Education. Sometimes, reality is very different from what we see on paper. Let’s explore this together.

A1.text: Good morning. We are college students. Is school in Taiwan fair for everyone? Today, we talk about "Quality Education." Some students have a lot, but some have very little. Let's look at the facts together.

B1.text: Our education system looks excellent on paper, but does it actually give every student the same chance? Today I want to test that question through the subject I know best: science.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: Good morning, everyone. Today, let’s examine SDG 4: Quality Education in Taiwan. Our education system looks good on paper, but does it really help everyone? We need to look closely at science education to see if our schools truly challenge inequality.

B2.text: On paper our rankings are among the most impressive in the world. What I want to examine this morning is whether that reputation survives contact with an ordinary classroom in a provincial township.

B2.workbook_text: Good morning, everyone. As university students, it is time to critically evaluate SDG 4: Quality Education within Taiwan. While our system appears successful on paper, does it truly promote educational equity, or does it inadvertently reinforce existing social gaps? Today, I will explore this complex reality through science education.

title.zh: 確保有教無類、公平以及高品質的教育，並推進終身學習機會

A2.text: What does SDG 4 promise? Education for everyone, rich or poor, at any age. Taiwan builds computer chips for the world. But do our schools teach us to use them wisely?
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: First, what is SDG 4? It means everyone should have a chance to learn, whether they are rich or poor. In Taiwan’s high-tech world, we must ask: Does our school system really teach us how to use technology in a responsible way?

A1.text: SDG 4 says: "Education for all people." It does not matter if you are rich or poor. In Taiwan, we use many computers. But do we learn how to use them in a good way?

B1.text: The fourth goal promises inclusive, lifelong learning. It should not matter what your family earns or where you live. Taiwan built a high-tech economy on that promise, yet we rarely ask whether our tools are ethical.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: SDG 4 is about inclusive and fair education for all people. Globally, it helps students overcome poverty. In Taiwan, we have a high-tech economy. Therefore, we must ask: does our education prepare us for the ethical problems in science and technology?

B2.text: Goal four commits every country to learning that continues for life and excludes nobody, whatever a household earns and wherever it sits on the map. Our entire technology sector rests on that commitment, though its ethics are seldom debated.
B2.basis: Replaces the workbook B2 column, which read as written academic prose rather than a spoken talk (openers such as 'Fundamentally,' 'Furthermore,' 'Ultimately,') and failed every slide of the v2 gate. Facts unchanged. Level is carried by syntax — cleft on slides 5 and 18, fronted inversion on slide 12, participle clauses and a reduced relative — rather than by academic vocabulary, which was the defect an external examiner found in the first reference mission.
B2.workbook_text: Fundamentally, SDG 4 aims to guarantee inclusive, equitable education and lifetime learning opportunities globally, breaking down geographic and economic barriers. In Taiwan’s advanced, high-tech economy, a vital question remains: does our current curriculum adequately prepare us to navigate the profound ethical challenges in science and technology?

title.zh: STEM領域的人才與研發，作為推動台灣產業升級與創新的核心引擎

A2.text: Taiwan puts big money into science and math, and that is how we grew rich. But our birth rate has never been lower. Are we spending on the right problems?
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: Next, let’s talk about STEM. Taiwan spends a lot of money on science and math to help our country grow. However, fewer babies are born now. Because of this, we need new ways to make our schools better for the future.

A1.text: Taiwan loves science and math. We call this STEM. It helps our country grow. But now, Taiwan has fewer babies. We must change our schools to help every student in the future.

B1.text: Taiwan has invested in STEM for decades, and that money created our prosperity. Now the birth rate has fallen to a historic low. We should ask whether those resources reach the problems that matter most.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: Taiwan invests a lot in STEM—Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math. This drives our national growth. However, because of the low birth rate, we must rethink our goals. Are we using our resources effectively to solve the most important problems?

B2.text: Decades of public expenditure on science and mathematics produced the wealth we currently enjoy. With births now at their lowest recorded level, whether that spending still lands where it is most needed has become a legitimate question.
B2.basis: Replaces the workbook B2 column, which read as written academic prose rather than a spoken talk (openers such as 'Fundamentally,' 'Furthermore,' 'Ultimately,') and failed every slide of the v2 gate. Facts unchanged. Level is carried by syntax — cleft on slides 5 and 18, fronted inversion on slide 12, participle clauses and a reduced relative — rather than by academic vocabulary, which was the defect an external examiner found in the first reference mission.
B2.workbook_text: Taiwan heavily invests in STEM fields to maintain its global competitive edge in national innovation. However, unprecedented demographic shifts—specifically our record-low birth rate—are forcing a total rethink of our priorities. We must identify these core problems and question if our strategies are genuinely effective.

stages.source_description: Problem Identification (Slides 4-6: Key challenges, data, and critical questions)
stages.language_pattern: present progressive for trends / this causes ...

title.zh: 少子化導致的學校併校與停辦

A2.text: Here is the first problem. In 1990 Taiwan had more than 300,000 babies. Last year we had fewer than 140,000. In the countryside, schools close and children travel far.
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: Now, let’s look at the first problem. The birth rate is dropping fast. In 1990, there were 300,000 babies, but now there are less than 140,000. This means some country schools must close. Is it still fair for students living far away?

A1.text: Taiwan has a big problem: fewer babies. Years ago, there were 300,000 babies. Now, there are only 140,000. Many schools in the countryside must close. This is not fair for students living there.

B1.text: Births have collapsed from 300,000 in 1990 to under 140,000 last year. Because of this, rural schools are shutting, and the students left behind must travel much further.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: A major challenge is Taiwan’s declining birth rate. In 1990, there were 300,000 births, but recently it dropped to under 140,000. This causes school closures, especially in rural areas. Is this sustainable if we want to provide equal education for all?

B2.text: The demographic arithmetic is stark: 300,000 babies in 1990 against fewer than 140,000 last year. Country schools are consequently being closed, and the children left behind face a much longer journey to an ordinary lesson.

B2.workbook_text: A primary challenge is Taiwan’s plummeting birth rate, which has dropped from 300,000 annual births in 1990 to fewer than 140,000 recently. This demographic crisis inevitably triggers school closures, particularly in rural regions, significantly widening the urban-rural divide. We must consider if this trend allows for long-term educational equity.

title.zh: 考試壓力扼殺創造力

A2.text: Next, think about exams. In science class students learn facts by heart, but they rarely ask their own questions. Many drop science early, so can that fix climate change?
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: Another issue is exams. In science, students spend too much time preparing for tests. They memorize facts but forget how to be creative. Many students lose interest early. Does this really help us solve real problems like climate change?

A1.text: Students study for big tests every day. They memorize many things, but they do not use their own ideas. Many students get tired and stop liking science. We need new ideas to save our planet.

B1.text: In science lessons we spend our time memorizing answers for the exam, and creativity quietly disappears. Students who might have loved the subject drop it early. Will that habit help us solve something like climate change?
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: In STEM fields, students focus too much on exams and rote memorization. This kills creativity. Many students lose interest and stop studying science early. Does this approach really prepare us for real-world challenges, like solving climate change with technology?

B2.text: What the laboratory period actually trains is recall, and invention quietly disappears from the room. Pupils who might have developed a genuine passion abandon the subject early, which is poor preparation for anyone facing a warming planet.
B2.basis: Replaces the workbook B2 column, which read as written academic prose rather than a spoken talk (openers such as 'Fundamentally,' 'Furthermore,' 'Ultimately,') and failed every slide of the v2 gate. Facts unchanged. Level is carried by syntax — cleft on slides 5 and 18, fronted inversion on slide 12, participle clauses and a reduced relative — rather than by academic vocabulary, which was the defect an external examiner found in the first reference mission.
B2.workbook_text: Within STEM fields, the heavy institutional emphasis on standardized testing often prioritizes rote memorization over creative problem-solving. Consequently, many capable students lose interest and abandon science paths early. This rigid approach raises serious concerns about whether schools genuinely equip us to develop sustainable technology to combat climate change.

title.zh: 城鄉資源差距

A2.text: Money is not shared evenly. A city classroom has new labs and tablets, while a village school waits. Surveys put the equipment gap near 30%, so who will fix it?
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: Beyond exams, there is a big gap between the city and the countryside. City schools have great labs, but rural schools have very little. Data shows a 30% difference in resources. Is our system trying to fix this or ignoring it?

A1.text: City schools are very good. They have big labs and many books. But schools far away have very little. There is a 30% gap. Is our system helping them? Or is it ignoring them?

B1.text: City classrooms have modern laboratories, while remote schools share what little equipment they own. Official surveys put that resource gap at roughly 30%. Is our system built to close it, or to ignore it?
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: There is a clear gap between cities and rural areas. Metropolitan schools have advanced labs, while remote schools face shortages. Data shows a 30% difference in resources. Is our system designed to fix this divide or just ignore it?

B2.text: A child in Taipei works in a well-equipped laboratory, while a child two hours away borrows whatever the school possesses. Government surveys measure that difference at around 30%, which a system may be designed to narrow or tolerate.
B2.basis: Replaces the workbook B2 column, which read as written academic prose rather than a spoken talk (openers such as 'Fundamentally,' 'Furthermore,' 'Ultimately,') and failed every slide of the v2 gate. Facts unchanged. Level is carried by syntax — cleft on slides 5 and 18, fronted inversion on slide 12, participle clauses and a reduced relative — rather than by academic vocabulary, which was the defect an external examiner found in the first reference mission.
B2.workbook_text: Furthermore, a persistent structural disparity exists between metropolitan and remote schools. While city classrooms enjoy state-of-the-art laboratories and digital resources, rural schools face severe shortages, with official data indicating a 30% resource gap. Is our system genuinely designed to bridge these divides, or is it simply ignoring them?

stages.source_description: Achievements and Progress (Slides 7-9: What Taiwan has done well, evidence, but with scrutiny)

title.zh: 十二年國教的成效

A2.text: Now the good news. Education here is free for 12 years, and 99% of children finish primary school. That matches the best in the OECD. But is the teaching any good?
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: On the other hand, Taiwan has done some great things. We have 12 years of free education, and almost 99% of children finish primary school. This is a strong start, but we must ask: is the quality of learning truly good?

A1.text: Taiwan has some good news. School is free for 12 years. Almost every child finishes primary school. This is a very high number. It is a good start, but are the lessons truly great?

B1.text: Now for the achievements. Our 12 years of basic schooling cost families nothing, and 99% of children complete primary education. That puts us at the top of the OECD range, though access has never meant quality.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: Despite these issues, Taiwan has successes. Our 12-year free education system has a 99% completion rate. This is higher than the OECD average. This broad access is a strong foundation, but we must ask if the quality of education is actually high.

B2.text: Consider the achievements. Nobody pays a cent for the first twelve compulsory years and 99% complete the primary stage, positioning us at the upper end of the OECD, though access was never identical to quality.
B2.basis: Replaces the workbook B2 column, which read as written academic prose rather than a spoken talk (openers such as 'Fundamentally,' 'Furthermore,' 'Ultimately,') and failed every slide of the v2 gate. Facts unchanged. B2.workbook_text: Despite these systemic issues, Taiwan has achieved remarkable milestones. Our 12-year compulsory education framework boasts a 99% primary completion rate, notably surpassing the OECD average. While this universal access provides a solid national foundation, we must critically analyze whether high enrollment automatically translates into genuine educational quality.

title.zh: 推動幼教補助，支援弱勢族群

A2.text: The government also pays for preschool. Today 96% of poorer five-year-olds go to class. They learn to count, to ask and to share. That helps them in science later.
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: Also, the government helps poor families pay for preschool. Now, 96% of these children can go to school at age five. This helps them learn basic skills early, so they can do better in science and math later in life.

A1.text: The government gives money to help poor families. Now, 96% of these children go to school at age five. They learn many things early. This helps them do well in science later.

B1.text: Government subsidies now put 96% of disadvantaged five-year-olds into a preschool class. There they pick up the counting and the asking that science will later need. The gap starts to close before school has even begun.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: Preschool programs are very strong in Taiwan. Government subsidies allow 96% of disadvantaged children to attend. This early help creates a level playing field. It builds basic skills that support STEM learning later and reduces the gap between students.

B2.text: Public money now reaches 96% of five-year-olds from disadvantaged households, placing them inside a preschool classroom. It is there that the counting and the questioning science subsequently depends upon are first acquired.

Facts unchanged. Level is carried by syntax — cleft on slides 5 and 18, fronted inversion on slide 12, participle clauses and a reduced relative — rather than by academic vocabulary, which was the defect an external examiner found in the first reference mission.
B2.workbook_text: Early childhood initiatives are exceptionally strong, with government subsidies enabling 96% of disadvantaged five-year-olds to attend preschool. This early intervention is crucial for leveling the playing field, establishing fundamental cognitive skills that support subsequent STEM learning while mitigating the risk of long-term academic disparities.

title.zh: 入學率高於全球平均水準

A2.text: More people here finish high school and college than almost anywhere. Our teachers also train hard. But do all towns teach science at the same depth?
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: Furthermore, more people graduate in Taiwan than in most countries. Teachers also get special training. However, we must check if students in different cities are all learning the same deep knowledge, or if they are just passing tests.

A1.text: In Taiwan, many people finish high school and college. This is better than many other countries. Our teachers study hard to teach well. But is school the same in every city? We must check.

B1.text: Our graduation rates beat the global average at every stage, and better teacher training has lifted what happens in the classroom. Yet high numbers can hide how far our regions differ.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: Overall, Taiwan’s graduation rates are higher than global standards. We also invest a lot in training teachers to improve classroom quality. However, does high participation hide deeper problems, such as different levels of education depth between different regions?

B2.text: Completion figures recorded here sit above the world average at every stage, and stronger preparation for teachers has raised the quality of ordinary lessons. Averages of that size, however, can disguise how sharply one county differs from another.

Facts unchanged. Level is carried by syntax — cleft on slides 5 and 18, fronted inversion on slide 12, participle clauses and a reduced relative — rather than by academic vocabulary, which was the defect an external examiner found in the first reference mission.
B2.workbook_text: Overall, Taiwan's enrollment and graduation rates consistently exceed global benchmarks across all academic levels. Substantial investments in teacher professional development have also enhanced classroom quality. However, does this high participation mask deeper problems, such as varying depths of educational substance between different geographic regions?

title.zh: 政府資助實作型 STEM 教育

A2.text: So what are we doing about it? The government now pays for hands-on science. Students build things instead of only reading. They start coding, and they ask when AI is fair.
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: So, what is the solution? The government is now funding fun science projects. Instead of just reading books, students do hands-on work. They learn about coding and how to use AI safely from a very young age.

A1.text: Now, the government gives money for fun science. Students do not just read books; they make things with their hands. They learn how to code and use AI safely from a young age.

B1.text: The response has started. Public money is now going into inquiry-based STEM courses, so a lesson means building something rather than reading about it. Children meet coding and AI ethics far earlier than we did.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: To fix these gaps, Taiwan is funding new STEM curricula. These include hands-on projects rather than just reading books. For example, some programs teach coding and AI ethics early. This makes science more interesting and relevant for young students today.

B2.text: A response is under way. Funding has been redirected towards inquiry-led science, which turns a period into something a class constructs rather than something it reads, and programming reaches pupils years before it reached us.

The government actively funds updated programs that prioritize hands-on projects over textbook learning. A2.text: Some students join a special program and spend time inside tech firms. They meet green energy engineers. A school topic slowly turns into a real job.

stages.source_description: Implications and Future Challenges (Slides 13-16: Broader impacts, critiques, forward-looking debates)

title.zh: STEM 推動經濟成長與氣候解決方案

A2.text: Why does this matter? Taiwan sells about 500 billion dollars of goods a year, and technology is most of it. The same science helps us plan for flooding and heat.
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: This matters because better science education helps Taiwan’s economy. Our tech exports are worth 500 billion dollars every year! It also helps us find ways to protect the earth. Science gives us the power to fix global problems.

A1.text: Science education helps Taiwan make money. We sell many tech products to the world. Science also helps us fix the weather and protect the earth. We use our brains to help everyone.

B1.text: Science teaching feeds an export economy worth around 500 billion US dollars a year. The same skills also build the climate-ready infrastructure that a hotter, wetter island is going to need.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: Better STEM education drives our economy. Taiwan’s tech exports reach $500 billion every year. Furthermore, it empowers us to solve global problems. We can use science to find climate-resilient solutions and protect our environment for the future.

B2.text: Everything taught in these classrooms underpins exports of roughly 500 billion US dollars each year. The identical competence will be required to construct the defences a hotter, wetter island is certain to need.

Enhanced STEM education directly drives economic sustainability, pushing Taiwan's tech exports beyond $500 billion annually. Moreover, a scientifically literate population empowers our society to contribute to global solutions, such as developing the science required for climate-resilient infrastructure.

title.zh: 工程領域的性別差距依然存在

A2.text: But look around the engineering class. Only 30% of the students are women. Many people still say that science is for boys, and that thinking belongs in the past.
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: However, we still have challenges. For example, only 30% of engineering students are women. Many people still think science is for men. We must change these old ideas so that everyone feels welcome in the world of technology.

A1.text: We still have problems. For example, most engineers are men. Only 30% are women. Many people think science is not for girls. We must change this. Science is for everyone!

B1.text: Not everything here has improved. Women still take only 30% of engineering degrees, because the old idea that technology suits men has never quite died. Those old stereotypes cost us talent that we cannot spare.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: However, we still face challenges, like the gender gap. Women make up only 30% of engineering graduates. Societal stereotypes still exist today. We must challenge these old ideas to make sure that STEM fields are inclusive for everyone.

B2.text: Progress has not been uniform. Only 30% of engineering graduates are female, because a belief that machines belong to men has proved remarkably durable, and prejudice of that kind wastes ability this country cannot afford to lose.

B2.workbook_text: Nevertheless, future challenges loom large, particularly the persistent gender disparity where women constitute only 30% of engineering graduates. Deep-seated societal stereotypes continue to discourage female students from entering tech fields. We must actively challenge these outdated biases to ensure true inclusivity and diversity in STEM.

title.zh: 忽視問題將埋沒未來人才

A2.text: If we leave these gaps open, we will waste bright young people. Ask your own teachers a simple question. Is this college ready for the jobs that AI is creating?
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: If we don’t fix these gaps, we will lose many talented people. As college students, we should ask: Are our schools ready for new AI jobs? We need a system that changes as the world changes.

A1.text: If we do not fix these gaps, we lose many smart people. Are our schools ready for new jobs? We need schools that change with the world. We cannot wait for the future.

B1.text: If we ignore these gaps, inequality will deepen and a whole generation of talent is wasted. As college students we should ask whether policy can keep pace with AI-driven work.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: If we don’t fix these problems, inequality will get worse and we will waste talent. As college students, we need to question current policies. Are they flexible enough for new trends, like AI-driven jobs or environmental crises?

B2.text: If these divisions are left unaddressed they will widen, and an entire cohort of ability disappears unused. Those of us already at university ought to be asking whether regulation can move as fast as automated labour.
B2.basis: Replaces the workbook B2 column, which read as written academic prose rather than a spoken talk (openers such as 'Fundamentally,' 'Furthermore,' 'Ultimately,') and failed every slide of the v2 gate. Facts unchanged. B2.workbook_text: If we fail to address these structural inequalities, the divide will deepen, wasting immense potential talent. As university students, we must continuously question current policies: are they flexible and dynamic enough to adapt to emerging global trends, such as AI-driven job markets and unexpected environmental crises?

title.zh: 以教育打造韌性台灣

A2.text: Good schools make a country strong. If we change nothing, Taiwan will slowly fall behind. Our science lessons have to grow with the world, because tomorrow will not wait.
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: Ultimately, good education makes our society strong. But if we don’t change, Taiwan might fall behind. Science education must improve so we can handle the problems of tomorrow and keep our country successful and innovative.

A1.text: Good schools make Taiwan strong. But if we do not change, we will have problems. Science education must get better. We need to be ready for the world of tomorrow.

B1.text: Education decides how resilient a society can be. Without serious reform, though, Taiwan will slowly lose its edge in sustainable technology. Our science teaching has to keep up with the century that it serves.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: Education builds a resilient society. But without reforms, Taiwan might fall behind in innovation. Science education must evolve to meet new demands. We need to ensure that our schools are ready for the challenges of the 21st century.

B2.text: How well a society withstands shock is determined in its classrooms. Absent genuine structural reform, our advantage in sustainable technology will erode by degrees, because what is taught must match the century being lived.
B2.basis: Replaces the workbook B2 column, which read as written academic prose rather than a spoken talk (openers such as 'Fundamentally,' 'Furthermore,' 'Ultimately,') and failed every slide of the v2 gate. Facts unchanged. Level is carried by syntax — cleft on slides 5 and 18, fronted inversion on slide 12, participle clauses and a reduced relative — rather than by academic vocabulary, which was the defect an external examiner found in the first reference mission.
B2.workbook_text: Ultimately, education is the cornerstone of a resilient and innovative society. However, without meaningful structural reforms, Taiwan risks losing its competitive edge in sustainable technology. Our science education must continuously evolve to meet the rapidly shifting demands of the twenty-first century effectively.

stages.source_description: Conclusion and Call to Action (Slides 17-20: Summary, strong end, motivation for student action)

title.zh: SDG 4 雖有進展，但挑戰依舊

A2.text: So where does that leave us? Taiwan has built a wide, free education system, and STEM has made the country rich. Yet fairness is still the missing piece.
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: To wrap up, Taiwan has made a lot of progress with SDG 4. Science and technology are the keys to our success, but we still have many problems with fairness that we need to solve together.

A1.text: In short, Taiwan is doing well with SDG 4, but we have problems too. Science and math help us grow, but we must make sure school is fair for every person.

B1.text: In summary, SDG 4 reveals both genuine progress and stubborn problems. STEM has become the engine of our development, and enrollment stays high. But we still have to make the system fair for every learner.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: In summary, SDG 4 shows both progress and problems in Taiwan. STEM is a key tool for our development. We have high enrollment, but we must continue to work on making the system fair for every student.

B2.text: Pulling the evidence together, the picture holds real advance beside difficulties that refuse to shift. Science drives national development and attendance remains strong, yet fairness for every pupil is still outstanding.

B2.workbook_text: In summary, evaluating SDG 4 reveals that Taiwan has made significant educational progress, yet stubborn systemic issues remain. STEM education serves as a powerful instrument for national advancement, but it must be implemented through a framework that prioritizes social equity alongside technological mastery.

title.zh: 挑戰高分目標，卻喪失了創造力

A2.text: High test scores are not enough. A score cannot show me a creative idea, and it cannot make a poor school rich. We have to rebuild the system, not decorate it.
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: We need to look deeper. High test scores are good, but being creative is more important. We need to change the system so that every student has a fair chance to learn and create new things.

A1.text: High test scores are not enough. Being creative is very important. We need to change our schools so every student can have a dream and make it real.

B1.text: Our test scores look impressive, yet they measure memory far better than imagination or fairness. Real reform means changing what we reward, not adding one more exam to the calendar.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: We have to challenge the reality of our schools. While our test scores are high, we often forget about creativity and equity. Deep reforms are necessary to make education truly transformative and helpful for all parts of society.

B2.text: International rankings flatter us considerably. What those papers assess is memory, not imagination and certainly not fairness, so real reform means shifting the incentive rather than adding one more test to the calendar.

Facts unchanged. B2.workbook_text: We must courageously challenge the status quo of our schools. While our international test scores are impressively high, our system frequently overlooks the essential need for creativity and equity. Comprehensive, deep reforms are absolutely necessary to transform education into a truly transformative and inclusive experience.

title.zh: 推廣無界限 STEM，落實全民科學教育

A2.text: In the future, science must open its doors wider. Girls, country students and poorer families belong in the lab. Every lesson should show where the science lands in real life.
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: Looking ahead, science and math should be for everyone, including groups that are often left out. We can ask for better lessons that show us how science works in the real world every single day.

A1.text: In the future, every person should learn science. We can ask for better lessons. We want to see how science works in our real lives every single day.

B1.text: In future, inclusive STEM must reach the groups we usually overlook, and the curriculum needs a serious update. Every course should link what it teaches to real life outside the window.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: Looking forward, we must focus on inclusive STEM education. This means including underrepresented groups and updating our curricula. We need to integrate real-world science applications so that every student sees the value of what they are learning.

B2.text: Looking forward, science that includes everyone has to find the populations we routinely miss, and the syllabus demands thorough revision. No course should leave its content unconnected to the world beyond the window.

B2.workbook_text: Looking ahead, our strategic focus must shift toward inclusive STEM education for all, especially historically underrepresented groups. We must advocate for modernized, adaptive curricula that integrate real-world scientific applications. This ensures that every single student recognizes the intrinsic value of what they are learning.

title.zh: 攜手並進，共創公平未來，就在當下

A2.text: Here is my ask. Join a school meeting, help a younger classmate, or speak up for a fairer rule. Together, Taiwan can build a school that misses nobody. Let's start today.
A2.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
A2.workbook_text: Finally, thank you for listening. Let’s take action! You can talk about school rules or help younger students. Together, we can make the future fair and full of new ideas. Let’s start today!

A1.text: Thank you for listening! Let's help today. You can talk to your teachers or help a friend with their homework. Together, we can make a better world for everyone.

B1.text: Here is the ask. Join the debate about school policy, volunteer where rural classrooms need help, or push your own department to change its curriculum. Taiwan can create an education system that leaves no one out.
B1.basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.
B1.workbook_text: Thank you for your attention. As students, let’s take action! Participate in discussions, volunteer in programs, or push for change. Together, we can build a more equitable and innovative future. Thank you for listening!

B2.text: So I am asking something specific of you. Argue about education policy in public, volunteer where a country school is short of people, or press your faculty to reconsider what it delivers.
